## Introduction

Forests can limit global warming because they can sequester carbon that would otherwise be atmospheric CO~2~ [@munro2025; @marvin2023; @smyth2014]. As such, forests are a key source for carbon credits [@gorain2025] and are increasingly being managed for carbon sequestration in addition to other management goals such as timber harvest, wildlife habitat, and recreation [@marvin2023]. Managing for carbon requires accurate estimates of current and future carbon stocks by principle [@munro2025] and, for managers seeking to sell carbon credits, by regulation [e.g., @arbcomp2013]. Therefore, accurate predictions of tree growth are necessary to accurately estimate biomass accumulation and carbon sequestration.

Forest growth and yield models are essential tools for predicting future carbon. Many possible growth and yield models exist, each with different histories, strengths, and weaknesses [@weiskittel2011]. By definition, models are necessary abstractions. Each model is designed using simplifying assumptions to enable prediction and inference. When using a model to inform management, these assumptions may lead to unrealistic or unexpectedly inaccurate results that could mislead decision-makers. Thus, it is essential to understand the assumptions underlying the particular models used for management, assess how assumptions affect model performance, and correct for those assumptions as necessary.

The Forest Vegetation Simulator (FVS) is a widely used collection of growth and yield models developed by the United States Forest Service [@crookston2005; @joo2025]. The Inland Empire variant of FVS (FVS-IE), covering western Montana, northern Idaho, and eastern Washington, was first developed as the Prognosis model for pure lodgepole pine (*Pinus contorta*) stands by @stage1973. @wykoff1990 further modified the model to include other common Rocky Mountain tree species (including western larch, *Larix occidentalis*, and Douglas-fir, *Pseudotsuga menziesii*), using data from \> 44,000 trees across the northern Rockies. FVS-IE has been regularly updated to use "best available" data [@dixon2002] since its initial development in the 70s, but the core logic of the model has remained the same (@fig-fvs-diagram). Large trees ($\geq$ 3" DBH) are projected forward in time by estimating basal area increment first, calculating diameter growth ($\widehat G_D$) from the basal area increment value, then predicting height increment (@fig-fvs-diagram). Basal area increment for each individual tree is estimated as squared inside bark diameter (DDS, calculated as $(D_\text{inside bark} + \widehat G_D)^2 – D_\text{inside bark}^2$) using a combination of site variables, competition metrics, and tree characteristics. An error, drawn from a normal distribution with mean 0 and variance based on the regression that developed the diameter growth model, is added to the estimate to allow random effects. The resulting value is then used alongside habitat type and initial tree size (DBH, notated as $D_0$, and height) to estimate height growth ($\widehat G_H$; @fig-fvs-diagram). The model's default coefficients for the diameter increment component of the model were originally developed using increment core data [@wykoff1990], whereas the coefficients for the height increment component of the model were originally developed using 10-year height measurements from a separate set of felled trees [@stage1975].

::: {#fig-fvs-diagram}
![](fvs_diagram.jpg)

FVS-IE core large tree growth model. From top to bottom: white boxes with solid outlines are input variables; black ovals are key model components estimated using input variables; white boxes with dashed outlines are optional keywords for calibration; and solid grey boxes are model outputs. Solid black arrows represent model processes that are always carried out. Calibration keywords (white boxes with dashed outlines) are numbered by the order in which they are applied. Dashed black arrows represent optional model processes. $D_t, \, H_t$ = diameter at time $t$ and height at time $t$, respectively, $\widehat G_D$ = FVS-predicted diameter growth, $\widehat G_H$ = FVS-predicted height growth, SF = scale factor, CCF = crown competition factor, BAL = basal area in larger trees, DDS = squared inside-bark diameter increment $(D_\text{inside bark} + \widehat G_D)^2 – D_\text{inside bark}^2$, similar to basal area increment.
:::

The large tree growth model relies on the assumption that tree growth is relatively homogeneous across stands that have the same site variables (elevation, slope, aspect, habitat type, and location code; @fig-fvs-diagram). However, FVS-IE has limited resolution in habitat type and location code because it is a regional growth model. Therefore, stands with identical site variables may still have meaningful variation in tree growth rates due to small-scale environmental factors [e.g., local climate; @erinsmith-mateja2025]. The violation of the assumption of homogeneous growth across local climates suggests that FVS-IE may inaccurately predict tree growth, volume, and carbon at single-stand scales. Though these prediction errors may average out across the entire IE region, FVS-IE is typically used to project one or a few stands at a time on a smaller geographic scale. This usage implies that stand-scale inaccuracies in FVS prediction accuracy could misinform management decision. The extent of this inaccuracy and methods for correcting for prediction errors are not well-known, yet they must be understood to ensure that FVS-IE can be a reliable tool for management.

Local calibration, or adjusting model outputs using a multiplicative or additive factor, can be an effective method for improving FVS accuracy [@cankaya2025; @swann2025; @cawrse2010; @diaz2018]. Presumably, this strategy is effective because it addresses the violation of the first assumption of homogeneity discussed above. The FVS-IE model architecture provides multiple ways to calibrate the large tree diameter growth model, including a built-in "self-calibration" routine that uses growth data provided with the input tree list.

Mechanisms for calibration (numbered boxes with dashed borders in @fig-fvs-diagram) differ by when in the projection cycle they are applied, what they are applied to, and how they attenuate. Calibration can take place before diameter/height increment projection (numbered boxes 1-5, including self-calibration in @fig-fvs-diagram) or after projections are made (numbered boxes 6 and 7; @fig-fvs-diagram). In the former case, adjustments to diameter growth rates affect projected height growth (@fig-fvs-diagram, see arrow labeled "10-year $\widehat G_D$"). In the latter case, adjustments to diameter do not affect height growth. The `READCORD` and `READCORH` keywords are applied before self-calibration (boxes 1, 4, and 2 respectively, in @fig-fvs-diagram), whereas `BAIMULT` and `HTGMULT` (boxes 3 and 5 in @fig-fvs-diagram) are applied after self-calibration. These methods of calibration also differ in whether they are additive or multiplicative. Self-calibrated scale factors, `READCORD`, and `READCORH` all represent intercepts added on the log-scale (boxes 1, 2, and 4 in @fig-fvs-diagram). In contrast, `BAIMULT` and `HTGMULT` function by multiplying untransformed basal area increment or height growth (boxes 3 and 5 in @fig-fvs-diagram). Calibration after projections are made must be done by multiplying untransformed diameter growth or height growth (boxes 6 and 7 in @fig-fvs-diagram). Unlike user-supplied scale factors (boxes 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 in @fig-fvs-diagram), self-calibrated scale factors (box 2 in @fig-fvs-diagram) gradually attenuate over the course of the simulation, causing long-term projections to approach model defaults. Because adding an intercept on the log-scale is equivalent to multiplying on the untransformed scale, I refer to both intercepts and growth multipliers as "scale factors." For a more in-depth discussion of scale factor selection and implementation, see @hamilton1994.

After selecting the appropriate keyword(s) to use to adjust tree growth to reflect local conditions, the scale factors themselves must be estimated. This step requires high-quality, consistently collected tree measurement data. Yet, tree growth data can be costly or difficult to obtain. Thus, the publicly available Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) national forest inventory (NFI) program is a promising source of calibration data. NFI data consist of tree measurements collected via a standard protocol every 5-10 years from field plots located across the country. There is one field plot for every \approx 24 km^2^ of forest, and each plot consists of a cluster of four 169 m^2^ subplots [@sampling2022a]. Due to this sampling design, FIA data are plentiful and spread across a wide variety of forest types, management histories, and environments. Furthermore, the breadth of this dataset provides the opportunity to go beyond the current literature of only estimating scale factors [e.g., @cankaya2025] and instead leverage a regression framework to quantify the effects of different local-scale variables on scale factor direction and magnitude. In this project, I use FIA data to understand how local variation affects FVS-IE prediction accuracy by estimating scale factors (i.e., the ratio of FIA-remeasured growth to FVS-predicted growth) in a Bayesian hierarchical model. I evaluate the fitted scale factor's ability to improve FVS-IE growth estimates, and I leverage the model framework to investigate how drought stress and site competition contribute to plot-level variation in FVS accuracy.

## Methods

Code in development is available on my GitHub: <https://github.com/sprachan/fvs-code/tree/main/fia_calib>. In that analysis code, I use an R package that I am currently developing (`rFVSIEtools` in the `fia-calib` code on my GitHub). This package is very much still in development, but source code is available at: <https://github.com/sprachan/FVSIE-tools> and the package can be installed with:

```{r}
#| eval: false

remotes::install_github('sprachan/FVSIE-tools')
```

### Data and Study Species

To evaluate how FVS-IE growth predictions deviate from actual tree growth, I used publicly available tree remeasurement data from Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) plots in western Montana and northern Idaho. To avoid confounding effects of plot history when investigating deviation due to local-scale variation, I only retained data from plots that had no recent disturbance or treatment history. I limited this analysis to Douglas-fir (*P. menziesii*) and western larch (*L. occidentalis*) growth because these are both common and commercially important species in the inland northwest. Both Douglas-fir and western larch are abundant in forests in the Northern Rockies, but the two species have different environmental specificity: Douglas-fir grows under a wider range of climate conditions [@psmesilvics] than does western larch [@laocsilvics].

To investigate how local-scale climate variables contribute to deviation from base FVS predictions, I used a gridded water balance model created by the National Park Service [@tercek2021; @tercek2023; @tercek]. This dataset includes annual and seasonal mean water balance parameters (estimated using methods from @lutz2010 and @thornthwaite1955) from 1981-2019 at 1km resolution. For this analysis, I used climatic water deficit from 1981-2019 as a climate predictor because it integrates a site's potential evapotranspiration relative to actual demand, serving as an indicator of drought stress. I used average water balance data over this time frame because trees are long-lived, so their growth integrates water balance parameters across long periods of time. However, FIA plot locations are fuzzed up to 0.8km on public lands and up to 1.6km on private lands for privacy. Thus, I calculated average climatic water deficit within 0.8km buffers around FIA plot locations on public lands and within 1.6km buffers around FIA plot locations on private lands.

### FVS Simulations

To generate uncalibrated FVS predictions, I ran FVS with self-calibration turned off. I simulated growth only for alive trees, turned tripling off (when tripling is on, FVS splits each tree record into three trees to stabilize random effects), and set the random seed to 2025 to ensure reproducibility.

### Modeling Scale Factors

Methods for calculating scale factors vary across the literature. FVS-IE uses median prediction error for self-calibration [@dixon2002]. Regression-based calibration has proven effective for the Southern variant of FVS [@cankaya2025] and the Central Rockies variant of FVS [@ex2014]. However, previous work has used linear regression exclusively to calculate scale factors by modeling some form of:

$$ \widehat D = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D $$

Where $\widehat D$ is the projected diameter after a certain period of time (i.e., the default FVS projection cycle length), $D$ is the remeasured diameter, and $\beta_i$ are regression coefficients. While this approach is effective, it fails leverage the ability of regression to quantify how plot and tree characteristics contribute to the magnitude and direction of calibration required. In contrast, I use regression to quantify how local-scale variation drives prediction error in FVS and how we may address this shortcoming.

To understand local-scale variables that contribute to deviation from "base" FVS-IE predictions and investigate spatial structure in deviation, I used a Bayesian hierarchical modeling (BHM) framework to model scale factors. The BHM approach formalizes the nested tree-within-plot structure, allowing each scale factor estimate to draw on information from the broader plot. I modeled the ratio of FIA remeasured basal area increment ($G$) to FVS projected basal area increment ($\widehat G$, @eq-gr) in relation to tree species, plot climatic water deficit (a proxy for drought stress), and stand density (in 1000 trees per hectare, a measure of crowding and thus competition).

$$G_r = \frac{G}{\widehat G}$$ {#eq-gr} Notice that

$$G = G_r\cdot \widehat G$$

So $G_r$ represents the empirical scale factor required to correct FVS estimates.

Note that I model scale factors in terms of basal area increment, not diameter increment, because most FVS scale factors are applied to basal area increment (@fig-fvs-diagram).

The hierarchical model for the scale factor for tree $i$ in plot $j$ (notated $G_{r, \, ij}$) is illustrated in a directed acyclic graph (@fig-dag).

::: {#fig-dag fig-pos="t"}
```{mermaid}
%%| fig-responsive: false
%%| fig-width: 6
flowchart BT

 B["$$\beta_{i,j}$$"] & C["$$\theta$$"] --> A(("$$G_{r, \, ij}$$"))

E{{"$$[l]_{ij}$$"}} &  F["$$\alpha_j$$"] & G["$$\beta_l$$"] --> B

H["$$\beta_E$$"] & I{{"$$E_j$$"}} & J["$$\beta_{\rho}$$"] & K{{"$$\rho_j$$"}} & L["$$\beta_0$$"] & M["$$\sigma_\text{plot}$$"]--> F
```

Directed acyclic graph representing the model for the scale factor $G_{r, \, ij} = \frac{G_{ij}}{\widehat G_{ij}}$ for tree $i$ in plot $j$; $G_{ij}$ represents remeasured basal area increment and $\widehat G_{ij}$ represents FVS-projected basal area increment. $[l]$ is a binary variable indicating whether or not tree $i$ is a larch, $D_{0, \, ij}$ is the initial diameter of tree $i$, $\alpha_j$ is a plot-specific intercept, $E_j = \frac{E_j-\overline E}{\text{sd}(E)}$ is standardized average water deficit for plot $j$, $\rho_j = \rho_j-\overline \rho$ is the centered initial density (in 1000s of trees per hectare) for plot $j$, $\beta_0$ is the plot adjustment when $E_j = \overline E$ and $\rho_j = \overline \rho$. $\sigma$ denotes a variance, with the subscript indicating the biological level that the variance enters the model. The response variable, $G_{r,\, ij}$, is in a circle, square boxes indicate parameters, and hexagons indicate predictors.
:::

Mathematically, I specified the model as:

$$G_r \sim \text{Gamma} \left(\mu_\text{tree} = \beta_{ij}, \theta \right)$$ {#eq-dg-model}

$$\beta_{ij} = \exp(\alpha_j +  \beta_l [l]) $$ {#eq-sf-model}

$$\alpha_j \sim \mathcal N(\mu_\text{plot} = \beta_0+\beta_E \cdot E_j +  \beta_\rho \cdot \rho_j, \text{ sd} = \sigma_\text{plot})$$ {#eq-plot-model}

Let us consider each level of the model in turn.

At the first level (@eq-dg-model), I modeled the scale factor for a single tree $i$ in a plot $j$ as a random variable that follows a Gamma distribution. I used the Gamma distribution because scale factors are strictly positive and I thought it reasonable for variance to be non-constant with regard to mean scale factors. Each empirical scale factor $G_r$ is drawn from a distribution with mean value $\beta_{ij}$, with dispersion quantified by the gamma scale parameter $\theta$. Note that the variance, $\sigma^2 = \theta\mu$, so the scale parameter indicates how the variance scales with the mean. Note also that $\theta > 0$.

The Gamma takes two parameters; let $\alpha$ denote the shape parameter and $\theta$ denote the scale parameter. Then, by moment matching, we can solve for these parameters in terms of the desired mean ($\mu_\text{tree}$), above:

$$\alpha = \frac{\mu}{\theta}$$

To calculate basal area increment, I first calculated basal area (ft^2^) from diameter (in) using the formula:

$$\text{Basal area} = \pi \left(\frac{1}{2} \cdot \frac{\text{diameter}}{12}\right)^2$$

FIA crews only remeasure diameter to the nearest 0.1". In consequence, if a tree grew less than 0.05" between measurements, the recorded diameter (and therefore the basal area) will be the same from first measurement to first remeasurement. This leads to 0 values in the response variable, which is not supported by the Gamma implementation in Stan. Thus, I calculated the likelihood for recorded basal area increment = 0 to be the gamma CDF (not pdf) from 0 to 0.05. For all other observations, I calculated the likelihood using the gamma pdf for that data value given the shape and scale parameters $\alpha$ and $\theta$ described above.

I calculated the mean scale factor value, $\beta_{ij}$, using the deterministic model described in @eq-sf-model where the mean is the combination of a plot-level effect ($\alpha_j$) and a larch effect ($\beta_l [l]$). Note that the larch effect is an additional intercept for western larches, so $\alpha_j$ indicates the plot-level effect for a Douglas-fir. I chose Douglas-fir as the "baseline" species because it is more prevalent. I exponentiated this linear combination because the scale factor must be strictly positive but I wished to allow positive, negative, or zero $\alpha_j$ and $\beta_l$.

At the next level, I modeled the baseline scale factor adjustment due to plot effects, $\alpha_j$ (@eq-plot-model). Each $\alpha_j$ is drawn from a normal distribution with mean given by $\beta_0 + \beta_E \cdot E_j +  \beta_\rho \cdot \rho_j$, where $E_j$ is the plot-level average annual climatic water deficit and $\rho_j$ is a measure of plot density (in total stand basal area, ft^2^). As described above, $E_j$ was standardized and $\rho_j$ was centered to improve computational efficiency and so that $\beta_0$ represented the average scale factor for a Douglas-fir in a stand with average density and deficit.

In summary, we are interested in the posterior $\mathbb P(\beta_{ij}, \sigma_\text{tree}, \beta_l,  \alpha_j, \beta_E, \beta_\rho, \beta_0, \sigma_\text{plot}|G_r)$. By Bayes theorem and conditional independence, we have:

$$\begin{split}
\mathbb P(\beta_{ij}, \theta, \alpha_j, \beta_E, \beta_\rho, \beta_l, \beta_0, \sigma_\text{plot}|G_r) \propto & \mathbb P(G_r|\beta_{ij}, \theta) \mathbb P(\beta_{ij}|\alpha_j, \beta_l ) \cdot\\ & \mathbb P(\alpha_j|\beta_E, \beta_\rho, \beta_0, \sigma_\text{plot}) \cdot \\ &\mathbb P(\theta)\mathbb P(\beta_l)\mathbb P(\beta_E)\mathbb P(\beta_\rho)\mathbb P(\beta_0)\mathbb P(\sigma_\text{plot})
\end{split}$$ {#eq-sf-posterior}

I specified weakly informative prior distributions for each parameter (@tbl-prior-distributions) designed to allow reasonable sampling efficiency while allowing the likelihood to be most informative. Note that the prior distributions for $\beta_{i,j}$ and $\alpha_j$ are given as @eq-sf-model and @eq-plot-model, respectively.

::: {#tbl-prior-distributions}
```{=latex}
\begin{tabular}{m{0.75in} p{1.5in} p{3.75in}}
\hline
Parameter & Prior Distribution & Justification \\ \hline
$\theta$ & half-Cauchy(0,1) & \small The scale parameter must be strictly positive, but I wanted to allow a fatter tail and more extreme values than the normal so that variance could increase substantially with the mean. \normalsize \\

$\sigma_\text{plot}$ & $\text{half-} \mathcal N(0, 1)$ & \small Standard deviations must be strictly positive, and I expected them to be small. \normalsize \\

$\beta_0$, $\beta_l$ & $\mathcal N(0, 0.5)$ & \small This prior softly constrains $e^{\beta_l}$ to be near 1, with room to wander towards 0 and out to about 3.5, which is more than enough room for scale factors (according to FVS documentation, scale factors should typically fall between 0.5 and 2.0).\normalsize \\

$\beta_E$, $\beta_\rho$ & $\mathcal N(0, 0.75)$ & \small Similar to $\beta_l$, but slightly less constrained. \\ \hline \normalsize
\end{tabular}
```

Prior distributions for estimated parameters. Note that $G_r$ has a log-linear relationship with $\beta_l$, $\beta_E$, and $\beta_\rho$, so a 1-unit change in $l$, $E$, or $\rho$ is associated with an $e^{\beta_i}$ multiplicative change to the scale factor.
:::

### Model Fitting and Checking

I fit the model described above using Stan version `{r} rstan::stan_version()` and rstan version `{r} packageVersion('rstan')`. I ran four chains of 3,000 iterations each, discarding the first 1,500 iterations as "warm-ups." Stan code is appended to this report after the references and is available on my GitHub (see @sec-code). I checked the model for convergence using traceplots and convergence diagnostics (Gelman and Rubin's $\hat R$, effective sample size). Additionally, I visualized pairwise joint posterior distributions of each parameters to explore parameter identifiability.

I used posterior predictive checks to evaluate if the model adequately captured patterns in the data. Specifically, given predictors $x$, I estimated $y_{rep}^{(i)}$ (the predicted $y$ values at iteration $i$) using the set of parameters $P^{(i)}$ at the same iteration. Then, I randomly selected six of these replicated datasets and compare the distribution of $y_{rep}^{(i)}$ to the observed distribution of $G_r$. To further quantify the alignment of these distributions, I compared the distribution of mean, median, maximum, and minimum values (from all the $y_{rep}^{(i)}$ datasets) to the actual values calculated from the observed data $y$.

### Prediction and Inference

I used visualization to evaluate the predictive accuracy of the model. Because I used the same dataset for prediction as for model training, I did not calculate metrics such as RMSE because these would be inaccurately small. The goal of the model was to estimate scale factors $\beta_{ij}$ such that $G_{ij} \approx \beta_{ij} \widehat G_{ij}$, so I wanted to visualize the relationship between $\beta_{ij} \widehat G_{ij}$ and $G_{ij}$. Therefore, I calculated posterior mean $\overline \beta_{i,j}$ for each tree $i$ in each plot $j$ and plotted $\overline\beta_{ij} \widehat G_{ij}$ against $G_{ij}$. If model performance was aligned with the modeling goal, the points on the scatterplot would fall roughly along the 1:1 line.

To support inference, I visualized the marginal posterior distributions for tree-level dispersion ($\theta$), plot-level variance ($\sigma^2_\text{plot}$), and each coefficient in my model. For coefficients in @eq-sf-model and @eq-plot-model, I exponentiated the raw posterior values in order to get the effective coefficient value. For example, a raw coefficient value of 0 would lead to an estimate of 1, so a 1-unit change in the predictor variable would have a 1x effect on the dependent variable (i.e., no detectable effect); a raw coefficient value of 0.69 would lead to a transformed estimate of 2, so a 1-unit change in the predictor variable would double the response variable. I calculated 95% credible intervals and posterior means for the listed parameters.

## Results

### Model Fitting and Checking

The HMC algorithm converged well, with no divergent transitions, no tree depth saturation, and large effective sample sizes. $\hat R >> 1.01$ for each parameter and the minimum $N_{eff}$ was \> 1400. Examining pairwise joint posteriors showed some correlation between $\beta_\text{larch}$ with the intercept, $\beta_0$ (@fig-joints), but other joint distributions were reasonably well-behaved.

::: {#fig-joints fig-height="10%" fig-pos="bh!"}
![](../../figures/lvl3_joint.png){fig-height="10%"}

Pairwise joint posterior distributions for all parameters. y axes are constant across rows, x axes are constant across columns. The most correlated parameters were the larch effect ($\beta_\text{larch}$) with the intercept ($\beta_0$) and $\sigma_\text{plot}$ with the scale parameter. All other pairwise comparisons did not show strong evidence of correlation (i.e., their joint distributions did not exhibit a "cigar" shape).
:::

Though the sampled posterior predictive datasets appeared roughly similar to the observed data, there were still key differences (@fig-post-pred-distribs). All predicted datasets had a slightly lower peak than the observed data, yet the observed data also had a slightly longer tail (@fig-post-pred-distribs).

::: {#fig-post-pred-distribs fig-pos="H"}
![](../../figures/post_preds.png)

Six randomly selected posterior predictive data distributions (blue), each compared to the observed data distribution (red). $G_r$ is the ratio of FIA remeasured basal area increment to FVS-projected basal area increment, $\frac{G}{\widehat G}$. Though distributions were similar, posterior data distributions were less skewed than the observed data, with lower peaks than the data and fewer extreme values. Panel labels indicate the randomly selected step in the MCMC algorithm that the posterior predictive data were drawn from.
:::

Despite the apparent similarity in posterior predictive datasets and the observed data in @fig-post-pred-distribs, the difference in skew between the two induced notable dissimilarity between key summary attributes of the posterior predictive datasets and the distribution of the observed data. The means, medians, and minima of posterior predictive distributions were relatively close to the observed data (within $\pm$ 0.03), though systematically overestimated (@fig-post-pred-checks). The model was not able to adequately capture the observed maximum basal area increment (@fig-post-pred-checks).

::: {#fig-post-pred-checks fig-pos="H"}
![](../../figures/post_pred_check.png)

Distributions of summary statistics from posterior predicted data (grey rectangles) compared to the observed value in the data (blue lines). $G_r = \frac{G}{\widehat G}$ is the ratio of FIA-remeasured basal area increment to FVS projected basal area increment. The distributions of mean, median, and minimum $G_r$ from posterior predictive data were somewhat similar to the observed values (within $\pm$ 0.05 ft$^2$), but were systematically overestimated by the model. In contrast, maxima calculated from each posterior predicted dataset were all substantially less than the observed data (top left panel).
:::

### Prediction and Inference

Unscaled FVS predictions generally over-predicted growth (@fig-sf-accuracy). Indeed, the posterior mean average scale factor for a Douglas-fir on a plot with average stand density and average deficit was 0.543, with relatively low uncertainty in this estimate (95% credible interval: 0.526 to 0.561; @fig-coef-posts), indicating that FVS-estimated basal area increment was, for an average plot, nearly double the remeasured values for Douglas-fir. Using posterior mean scale factors ($\overline \beta_{ij}$, @eq-plot-model) appeared to reduce FVS prediction bias (@fig-sf-accuracy). Predictions were about equally well scaled for both species, unlike unscaled FVS predictions, which were more biased for Douglas-fir than western larch (@fig-sf-accuracy). Additionally, scaled predictions appeared less variable than unscaled predictions (i.e., a tighter spread about the 1:1 line). However, scaled predictions for fast-growing trees (true basal area increment $\gtrapprox$ 0.5 ft$^2$) were still relatively inconsistent with reality.

::: {#fig-sf-accuracy fig-pos="H"}
![](../../figures/lvl3_scaled_preds.png)

Unscaled (left column) and model-scaled (right column) basal area increment predictions from FVS plotted against remeasured basal area increment, separated by species (top row is Douglas-fir, bottom row is western larch). In all panels, the solid black line is the 1:1 line and the dashed grey line is a simple linear model to help visualize the patterns in the data (not for inference or prediction). Points from an unbiased, well-fitting model would show random scatter about the 1:1 line, and the simple linear model would be similar to the 1:1 line. (Left column) Before scaling, basal area increment was generally over-predicted by FVS, though growth in trees with larger measured basal area increment were under-predicted (i.e., most points fall above the solid black line, but some fall below it toward the right end of the x-axis). Unscaled FVS was more accurate for larches than Douglas-firs (top vs bottom panel). (Right column) Scaling using modeled scale factors resulted in generally more accurate predictions, but the scaling procedure still led to systematic underpredictions for trees with large basal area increment in both species.
:::

Plot-level predictors (stand density and deficit) had little effect compared to the scale factor for an average density, average density plot. Each square foot of stand basal area above the average value adjusted the scale factor by only $\approx$ -1% per additional square foot of basal area ($\text{exp}(\overline \beta_\rho)=0.989$), and this coefficient estimate was associated with extremely low uncertainty (95% credible interval: 0.991 to 0.986; @fig-coef-posts). Though the estimated effect of deficit was more uncertain (95% credible interval: 0.936 to 0.995), the effect is also likely to be small ($\text{exp}(\overline \beta_\text{evap}) = 0.965$, or about a 3% decrease in scale factor per standard deviation of deficit; @fig-coef-posts). If the tree was a larch, however, the average scale factor would be increased by just over 20% ($\text{exp}(\overline \beta_\text{larch}) = 1.21$; @fig-coef-posts) and become closer to 1 (no scaling necessary). This estimate was somewhat uncertain (95% credible interval: 1.16 to 1.26), but the effect is relatively large on the multiplicative scale. For example, the average scale factor for a larch on a plot with average stand density and average deficit would be about 0.657, instead of the 0.543 for a Douglas-fir.

::: {#fig-coef-posts fig-pos="H" fig-height="30%"}
![](../../figures/lvl3_coefs.png)

Posterior distributions for regression coefficients (@eq-dg-model and @eq-sf-model). In all panels, the blue line is the posterior mean and blue shading is the 95% symmetric credible interval. Note that these coefficients have been exponentiated, so they should be interpreted as the multiplicative change that occurs in the response variable (scale factor) that results from a one-unit increase in the predictor. beta_0 is the intercept, representing the average scale factor for a Douglas-fir on a plot with average stand density and deficit, beta_density is the coefficient for centered total stand basal area, beta_evap is the coefficient for standardized (centered and divided by standard deviation) climatic water deficit, and beta_larch is the additional larch-specific intercept.
:::

Scale, the parameter representing how variance scales with the mean scale factor at the tree-level, was small ($\overline \theta = 0.220$, 95% credible interval: 0.212 to 0.228; @fig-dispersion-posts). However, plot-level standard deviation was large (posterior mean of $\text{exp}(\overline \sigma_\text{plot}=1.47$), though somewhat uncertain (95% credible interval: 1.47 to 1.51, @fig-dispersion-posts).

::: {#fig-dispersion-posts fig-pos="H"}
![](../../figures/lvl3_vars.png)

Posterior distributions for dispersion parameters (@eq-dg-model and @eq-sf-model). In all panels, the blue line is the posterior mean and blue shading is the 95% symmetric credible interval. Plot-level standard deviation ($\sigma_\text{plot}$) was exponentiated because plot error was added on the log-scale (@eq-sf-model). Scale is the measure of how tree-level variance in scale factor scales with mean (i.e., $\sigma^2_\text{tree} = \text{scale}\cdot \mu_\text{tree}$). $\sigma_\text{plot}$ represents plot-level standard deviation in the estimated scale factors, $G_r$.
:::

## Discussion

Overall, the hierarchical model for scale factors seemed to be better suited for adjusting estimates than illuminating the causes for adjustment. However, posterior predictive checks indicated that the model was unable to accurately capture key aspects the extreme skew of the data. Most $G_r$ values are small: 75% of values are below 0.69 and 99% of values fall below 2.21, but the maximum observed $G_r$ value was 7.92. The priors on coefficients were more forgiving than FVS' suggestion that scale factors should fall between 0 and 2, but they placed near-zero probability on scale factors as large as 7.92. I think it likely that the 7.92 value is the result of an issue with the FIA data (recorded incorrectly in the FIA database, measured on a decayed tree but not recorded as such, or simply measured incorrectly). Nonetheless, a model adequately representing the data generating process should still be able to capture maximum $G_r$ values near 6 (the next highest $G_r$ value is 5.7), and most posterior predictive data distributions had smaller maximum values. Thus, either a wider prior distribution for the intercept ($\beta_0$) or a likelihood model with a different variance structure (e.g., the lognormal, where variance increases with mean squared instead of the gamma, where the variance increases linearly with the mean) may improve the model's ability to replicate the skew of the data. Including initial diameter as a predictor variable may also help model the skew of the data. Tree growth changes as trees get larger, and it is possible that FVS does not accurately capture this relationship in our region or for certain areas of our region. Thus, including initial diameter as a predictor after more closely examining extreme values in the data could improve the model's ability to recover the data distribution.

Another indicator that the likelihood model fails to capture the variation in the data is the extremely high plot-level variance estimated by the model and the low contributions of stand density and deficit to the average scale factor estimate. If the model for the plot-level mean scale factor (@eq-sf-model) captured key drivers of plot-level FVS performance variation, I would expect to see relatively small estimates for plot standard deviation. Because I am interested in the causes of plot-to-plot variability, I will build on the model developed in this report by exploring alternative plot-level predictor variables, as well as testing the usefulness of a spatial covariance structure to the model's ability to recover the data distribution.

Modeled scale factors improved prediction accuracy, but they did not fully eliminate model bias. As with unscaled FVS, scaled predictions were still somewhat high for trees that did not grow as much, but somewhat low for trees that grew more. This could be a symptom of a model that inadequately accounts for the variation in growth rate due to initial size. Nevertheless, this result suggests that the model's inability to capture extreme values of the data does not compromise its potential use for producing scale factors for FVS users. I will test the generalizability of the model's scale factors by applying them to tree growth data at Lubrecht Experimental Forest and a selection of non-FIA permanent growth plots across the study region.

## Stan Code

```stan
functions{
  real gamma_zeroes_lpdf(vector y, vector shape, real rate){
    vector [num_elements(y)] llk;
    for(i in 1:num_elements(y)){
      if (y[i] == 0) 
        // recorded DG = 0 means actual could be anywhere from 0-0.05.
        llk[i] = gamma_lcdf(0.05|shape[i], rate); 
      else
        llk[i] = gamma_lpdf(y[i]|shape[i], rate);
    }
    return sum(llk);
}
}

data {
  int<lower=0> N;
  int<lower=0> N_plots;
  vector<lower=0>[N] G_r;
  vector[N] larch; // binary indicator on species ID
  array[N] int plot_id;
  vector[N_plots] evap;
  vector[N_plots] density;
}


parameters {
  // tree level parameters
  real<lower=0> scale;
  real beta_larch;
  
  // plot parameters
  real beta_evap;
  real beta_density;
  real beta_0;
  real<lower=0> sigma_plot;
  vector[N_plots] alpha_plot_std;
}

transformed parameters{
  vector[N_plots] alpha_plot = beta_0+beta_evap.*evap+beta_density.*density + 
                                sigma_plot.*alpha_plot_std;
  vector[N] mu = exp(alpha_plot[plot_id]+beta_larch.*larch);
  vector[N] shape = mu/scale;
}

model {
  // tree-level priors
  scale ~ cauchy(0, 1); // draw one value total
  beta_larch ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  
  // plot-level priors
  beta_evap ~ normal(0, 0.75);
  beta_density ~ normal(0, 0.75);
  beta_0 ~ normal(0, 0.5); 
  alpha_plot_std ~ std_normal();
  sigma_plot ~ normal(0, 1); 

  // data model
  G_r ~ gamma_zeroes(shape, 1/scale);
}

generated quantities {
  array[N] real y_rep = gamma_rng(shape, 1/scale);
}
```
